items.pull_quote: during the week you’d stay with your grandparents and then on the weekends you’d stay with your mom
items.summary: Bryant supplied the arrangement of Liston's Kansas City childhood, weekdays with her grandparents and weekends with her mother.
items.about: childhood living arrangements in Kansas City
items.notes: Liston's reply block opens with a long transcriber summary; her own words are only the last sentence.

items.pull_quote: She was overqualified for the work that she was getting.
items.summary: Bryant explained that Liston's mother had been overqualified for the work she could get in Kansas.
items.about: her mother's work and the move west

items.pull_quote: At your home, I know you said you had a piano – a piano-roll piano. So you were exposed to that. And you had a radio, and you were exposed to the music that you heard that was being played around Kansas City.
items.summary: Bryant recounted Liston's early exposure to music through a player piano and the radio at home in Kansas City.
items.notes: Liston points out it is the same piano she still owns.

items.pull_quote: your teachers thought you were a genius, and the church members too thought you were a genius, because you could do that. But it’s something that your little mind told you – which was great.
items.summary: Bryant recalled that Liston's childhood system for picking out melodies by scale number had made her teachers and church members think her a genius.
items.about: her childhood ear and number system for melodies

items.pull_quote: You found that you couldn’t reach the sixth and the seventh position on it, but you overcame that by . . .
items.summary: Bryant set up the story of the child Liston being too small to reach the sixth and seventh slide positions, and Liston finished the sentence.
items.about: reaching the far trombone positions as a child
items.notes: Liston completes the sentence: '. . . turning my head sideways.' A good paired exchange.

items.pull_quote: In 1937 all of a sudden the family moved to California.
items.summary: Bryant dated the family's move to California to 1937.
items.notes: Liston corrects the sequence: her grandmother and aunts went first, she and her mother followed months later.

items.pull_quote: you passed a test to be in the ninth grade?
items.summary: Bryant recalled Liston saying she had tested into the ninth grade though she was too young for it.

items.pull_quote: Miss Hightower seemed to have had quite an attachment. She thought you were just the greatest.
items.summary: Bryant told Liston that her teacher Miss Hightower had been attached to her and thought her the greatest.
items.notes: Liston: 'I don’t know about that.' Bryant presses: 'It’s been said.' (295570).

items.pull_quote: But you had mentioned yesterday that you would do some skits sometimes with Pigmeat Markum?
items.summary: Bryant recalled that Liston had done stage skits with the comedian Pigmeat Markum at the Lincoln Theater.

items.pull_quote: That must have been an education, working with him.
items.summary: Bryant remarked that working with Pigmeat Markum must have been an education for the young Liston.

items.pull_quote: But your first job, you said, with him was at Shepp’s Playhouse.
items.summary: Bryant placed Liston's first job with Gerald Wilson at Shepp's Playhouse.

items.pull_quote: Oh that’s where – you got stranded there.
items.summary: Bryant recalled that the band backing Billie Holiday was stranded in the South.
items.notes: Liston's fuller account of the stranding is at 295633.

items.pull_quote: Gerald said that you recorded with Basie and that the record is out now, on CD.
items.summary: Bryant passed on Gerald Wilson's statement that Liston had recorded with Count Basie and that the record was out on CD.
items.notes: Liston's reply is only a transcriber summary: she does not know about it or remember recording with Basie. Bryant returns to it at 295932 ('I think that Basie thing was on a 78').

items.pull_quote: Because you got tired of the road.
items.summary: Bryant suggested Liston took the Board of Education job because she was tired of the road.
items.about: leaving music for the Board of Education
items.notes: Liston: 'Not so much tired of it.' Then agrees it was the conditions (295667).

items.pull_quote: You sounded good.
items.summary: Bryant told Liston she sounded good on her 1947 recording date with Dexter Gordon.
items.notes: Follows Liston's 'That was terrible' (295689) about her first time playing without music. The rest of 295690 is bracketed.

items.pull_quote: Yeah. You broke the ice. You were the innovator.
items.summary: Bryant told Liston she had broken the ice as a woman trombonist and was the innovator.
items.about: being the first woman trombonist audiences saw
items.notes: Liston gives the credit to Gerald Wilson instead.

items.pull_quote: was that the ’56 band with Dizzy, where the guys were saying, why’d you send across to the West Coast to get a you-know-what?
items.summary: Bryant recalled the 1956 Gillespie band members grumbling about Dizzy sending to the West Coast for a woman.

items.pull_quote: Dizzy said it was because some of them had friends that they wanted to play, to take that spot, and he sent and got you.
items.summary: Bryant reported Dizzy Gillespie's account that band members wanted the chair for their friends but he sent for Liston.
items.notes: Liston tells the 'take one of those arrangements out' story in reply.

items.pull_quote: he relished telling that story, because it confirmed what he felt about – the faith that he had in you.
items.summary: Bryant said Dizzy Gillespie relished telling how Liston's arrangement silenced the band, because it confirmed his faith in her.
items.notes: Liston: 'He was so good. I was there until the band broke up.'

items.pull_quote: Was that when the work started falling off and Lorraine told him it was the band or her?
items.summary: Bryant asked whether the Gillespie band ended when work fell off and Lorraine Gillespie gave Dizzy an ultimatum.
items.about: the end of Gillespie's big band
items.notes: Liston corrects: 'It stopped. Not falling off. It stopped.'

items.pull_quote: I heard how you got the kids to start to read music, to become interested in jazz, and how you got the school systems down there . . .
items.summary: Bryant praised what she had heard of Liston's work in Jamaica getting children reading music and interested in jazz.
items.notes: Liston: 'I didn’t get the school systems.' ... 'The students I got.'

items.pull_quote: But he didn’t resent your music.
items.summary: Bryant stated that Liston's husband had not resented her music.
items.notes: Liston: 'No. He was glad for my music.'

items.pull_quote: because I know that’s what we went through.
items.summary: Bryant identified with Liston's story of harassment on the road as what women musicians of their generation went through.
items.about: harassment of women on the road
items.notes: Responds to Liston's 'that’s what girls have to go through' (295773). The block contains a short [?] gap before this phrase; the quote avoids it.

items.pull_quote: That was after Dizzy’s – somebody’s band broke up and this agent said, “You don’t have to be without work. You take a girl’s group” to wherever, and that’s the way that started.
items.summary: Bryant told how an agent suggested Liston take a women's group after a band broke up, which began her all-women group.
items.notes: Liston's reply (295785) is only a transcriber summary.

items.pull_quote: I know, but it was an important something.
items.summary: Bryant insisted that Liston's film work mattered after Liston dismissed it as 'just something'.
items.notes: Liston: 'You make too much of these . . .' Bryant: 'No, I’m not making too much. That’s important.' (295817).

items.pull_quote: Yeah, Major Holley. You’re always talking about him. He talked about you the whole time . . .
items.summary: Bryant recalled that bassist Major Holley, whom Liston always talked about, talked about her the whole time too.
items.notes: Liston: 'He bought my first – the first computer that I had.'

items.pull_quote: A lot of your arrangements, are they Ellington-inspired? I get some nuances in some of your stuff, the way you lay it out.
items.summary: Bryant said she heard Ellington-like nuances in the way Liston laid out her arrangements.
items.notes: Liston: 'I do it all from my soul, and if it sounds like somebody, well it sounds like somebody.'

items.pull_quote: But he liked it.
items.summary: Bryant affirmed that Thelonious Monk liked what Liston wrote for him.
items.notes: Liston calls writing for Monk 'a great honor'.

items.pull_quote: Because you probably already know before he says it, after 40 years.
items.summary: Bryant suggested that after forty years Liston knew what Randy Weston wanted before he said it.
items.notes: Liston: 'He says I write like he writes.'

items.pull_quote: You’re really reaching down.
items.summary: Bryant said Liston was really reaching down in writing her first piece for trombone and strings.
items.about: her new piece for trumpet, trombone and strings
items.notes: Liston: 'You’ve got to reach down on everything.'

items.pull_quote: That was obvious at the rehearsals for the Groove Festival. They would be waiting for you.
items.summary: Bryant recalled seeing at the Groove Festival rehearsals how many musicians were waiting for Liston to write for them.
items.about: demand for her writing in New York

items.pull_quote: Because you used to say, whenever you would be sad or something, you’re horn would bring you out of it, but now you can’t depend on that, so Randy is your horn right now.
items.summary: Bryant recalled Liston saying her horn used to lift her out of sadness, and said that after the stroke Randy Weston had become her horn.
items.about: the horn, the stroke and Randy Weston
items.notes: Same block also says 'You’ve written for everybody. You played with everybody.' Liston answers the goals question instead: 'I haven’t mad no money.'

items.pull_quote: they’ll be ready for you, and they won’t be piddly-paddling with the money.
items.summary: Bryant predicted that New York would be ready for Liston and would pay her properly.
items.about: money and the move back to New York

items.pull_quote: You helped establish the Pittsburgh Jazz Orchestra in Pennsylvania in 1964, and then you – the Harlem Backstreet Tour Orchestra.
items.summary: Bryant credited Liston with helping establish the Pittsburgh Jazz Orchestra in 1964 and the Harlem Backstreet Tour Orchestra.
items.notes: Same block also names the Pratt Institute Youth in Action.

items.pull_quote: On your first one you had Bennie Green, Al Grey, Benny Powell.
items.summary: Bryant listed Bennie Green, Al Grey and Benny Powell on the first Melba and Her 'Bones record date.
items.about: the Melba Liston and Her 'Bones record
items.notes: Liston: 'No, I had girls first.' (She is talking about the band, not the record.)

items.pull_quote: does it strike you funny, with all your experiences and your writing, technique, and expertise in doing so many – on your horn and everything – does it strike you funny or kind of sad that a large record company has never signed you to a contract?
items.summary: Bryant asked whether it struck Liston as sad that, for all her expertise, no large record company had ever signed her.
items.about: never being signed by a major label
items.notes: Liston: 'I’m a woman. That’s that.'

items.pull_quote: I think I read where you said that the women were amazed that you could be up there doing what you were doing, and they weren’t allowed the freedom.
items.summary: Bryant recalled reading that women in the Middle East on the State Department tour were amazed to see Liston on the bandstand.

items.pull_quote: that your arrangement on My Reverie – no, Anitra’s Dance – Annie’s Dance would break the ice, because there was – they recognized the theme and they liked your arrangement – treatment of it.
items.summary: Bryant reported that on the State Department tour Liston's Annie's Dance broke the ice with audiences who recognised the theme.
items.about: Annie's Dance on the State Department tour

items.pull_quote: you wrote a compilation of music for this tour that included excerpts from Duke and Basie and all those people.
items.summary: Bryant stated that Liston wrote the compilation of Ellington and Basie excerpts for the State Department tour.
items.notes: Liston: 'it was nothing for me to take a little bit of this and a little bit of that.'

items.pull_quote: They had a lot of respect for you then.
items.summary: Bryant said the stars Liston worked for must have had a lot of respect for her.
items.about: how Ray Charles and Dinah Washington treated her
items.notes: Liston: 'I guess so.'

items.pull_quote: I’ve seen Ray and Dinah go off on people for no reason. You’re better at music. You didn’t have that problem.
items.summary: Bryant said she had seen Ray Charles and Dinah Washington turn on people, but Liston never had that problem.
items.about: working with Ray Charles and Dinah Washington

items.pull_quote: Austin Cromer sings your arrangement of If You Could See Me Now. That was great.
items.summary: Bryant introduced Austin Cromer's recording of Liston's If You Could See Me Now arrangement and called it great.
items.about: her If You Could See Me Now arrangement
items.notes: Bryant asks if she gets thrilled; Liston: 'Sometimes.'

items.pull_quote: Just sometimes? This should have been one of the times.
items.summary: Bryant insisted that the If You Could See Me Now arrangement should have thrilled Liston.
items.about: her If You Could See Me Now arrangement
items.notes: Draws Liston's 'I watch you getting thrilled, and then I get a thrill from that.'

items.pull_quote: you should have seen the expressions on the whole
items.summary: Bryant recalled playing Liston's arrangements for visiting Basie band members and seeing their expressions.
items.about: how other musicians reacted to her arrangements
items.notes: The block also says 'That was beautiful.' Liston answers the follow-up question about who suggested the tune.

items.pull_quote: But I liked the way you do your shadings. The trumpets blare out and you drop it down and the reeds are under, and then the trumpets are – that’s – to me that’s kind of a lost art in arrangement.
items.summary: Bryant praised Liston's dynamic shadings, trumpets blaring then dropping under the reeds, as a lost art in arranging.
items.notes: Liston: 'I guess so.' Then: 'I still write like that.' (296071).

items.pull_quote: But doesn’t that go back to when Mrs. Hightower was teaching you – I know she taught you. That’s an old-school type thing.
items.summary: Bryant traced Liston's sense of building an arrangement back to Mrs. Hightower's old-school teaching.

items.pull_quote: And boy, you had your wind power there. You get a long stretch without a breath there. I kept waiting for you to breathe.
items.summary: Bryant marvelled at Liston's breath control singing You'll Be Sorry.
items.about: her singing on You'll Be Sorry
items.notes: Liston: 'no problem there, when I was young.'

items.pull_quote: And then one phrase there you really sounded like Billie Holiday.
items.summary: Bryant told Liston that one phrase of her singing on You'll Be Sorry sounded like Billie Holiday.
items.about: her singing on You'll Be Sorry
items.notes: Liston: 'Oh yeah?' Bryant expands in 296097.

items.pull_quote: the fill-ins behind the phrases of the words and then behind Dizzy when he’s playing, that’s perfect. Just beautiful.
items.summary: Bryant called the fill-ins in Liston's You'll Be Sorry arrangement, behind the vocal and behind Dizzy's solo, perfect.
items.notes: Same block: 'your nuance was strictly Billie'. Liston: 'Thank you.'

items.pull_quote: That is really a beautiful arrangement on that.
items.summary: Bryant called Liston's Annie's Dance arrangement for Gillespie's band really beautiful.
items.notes: Liston: 'It’s still good.'

items.pull_quote: we’ve heard three different styles of your writing, because everybody refers to you as a ballad-type person, melodic and all that stuff, but you’ve thrown in the blues, and then you’ve thrown in this production.
items.summary: Bryant said the recordings showed three styles of Liston's writing, against her reputation as only a ballad writer.
items.notes: Liston: 'I thank you.'

items.pull_quote: When you edit it down, boy, it’s together. Whatever you take out, I don’t think it belongs in there. Whatever you leave in, it goes.
items.summary: Bryant praised how tight Liston's arrangements were after editing.
items.notes: Bryant's thought continues into 296134 before Liston's 'Yeah.'

items.pull_quote: that is one of the most beautiful things you’ve ever done – especially the haunting sound that you get on your trombone and what you write behind what you’re doing.
items.summary: Bryant told Liston that My Reverie was one of the most beautiful things she had ever done, for her haunting trombone sound and the writing behind it.
items.notes: Same block: 'Hey that’s so pretty it makes you want to cry, Melba.' (inside the block after a bracket) and that Dizzy 'must have been thinking about Melba'. Liston: 'I don’t know.'

items.pull_quote: Anybody plays like that, got to be thinking about something.
items.summary: Bryant insisted that anyone who played like Liston on My Reverie had to be thinking about something.
items.about: what she thought about while playing My Reverie
items.notes: Liston: 'I got to be thinking about the notes, man.'

items.pull_quote: And the arrangement – you set yourself up so good.
items.summary: Bryant said Liston's My Reverie arrangement set up her own solo perfectly.

items.pull_quote: Well, you’re one in a million.
items.summary: Bryant gave up pressing and told Liston she was one in a million.
items.notes: Liston: 'Oh, boy. If I could do that that now.'

items.pull_quote: Because I want to hear you again Melba.
items.summary: Bryant told Liston she wanted to hear her play again.
items.about: her return to the trombone after the stroke

items.pull_quote: Those two or three notes, you can take them and do something magical with them.
items.summary: Bryant said Liston could make something magical of the two or three notes she could still play after the stroke.
items.notes: Liston explains the trouble with her arm.

items.pull_quote: Because that was a beautiful solo, Melba.
items.summary: Bryant praised Liston's trombone solo on a Randy Weston waltz recorded in Montreal.
items.about: her solo on a Weston ballad
items.notes: Liston: 'Thank you.' and then recalls the Montreal session.

items.pull_quote: You sure knew what to do. And your voicings on those strings. That’s beautiful. It’s the first time I heard you write for strings, Melba. That’s beautiful. And I’ve heard a lot of people try to write for strings, and it doesn’t have that kind of sound.
items.summary: Bryant praised Liston's string voicings on the Earth Birth Little Niles, saying others who write for strings do not get that sound.
items.about: her string writing on Little Niles
items.notes: Liston answers by pointing to her earlier Gloria Lynne string writing.

items.pull_quote: That treatment of Little Niles is very unique. It’s different and it’s good. It’s bad. It’s bad, Melba. Very good.
items.summary: Bryant called Liston's strings treatment of Little Niles unique and 'bad' in the jazz sense.
items.notes: Liston: 'I didn’t hear anything different than . . .'

items.pull_quote: We heard the original, and the strings, and this one, and they’re all completely different. You arranged all of them.
items.summary: Bryant said the three versions of Little Niles Liston arranged were all completely different.
items.notes: Liston: 'Not quite different.'

items.pull_quote: You’re getting royalties and all – air play and stuff. That’s great.
items.summary: Bryant assumed Liston was earning royalties and airplay from Weston's repeated recordings of her arrangements.
items.notes: Contrast Liston's earlier 'I haven’t mad no money.' (295939). Liston had said 'Oh yeah.' (296266) to Bryant's preceding money remark.

items.pull_quote: the strings is really a completely huge dimension to your writing that I’d never heard before, Melba.
items.summary: Bryant said the 1996 Hi-Fly showed string writing as a huge dimension of Liston's work she had never heard before.
items.notes: Liston: she has been writing for strings as long as for horns (296274).

items.pull_quote: I heard it. I just didn’t know that was you writing it then.
items.summary: Bryant admitted she had heard Liston's 1959 Gloria Lynne string writing without knowing it was Liston's.
items.about: uncredited string writing for Gloria Lynne
items.notes: Liston: 'Yeah. I guess not.' Bears on credit and recognition.

items.pull_quote: You guys are so in tune to each other, you don’t need – he doesn’t have to tell you anything anyway.
items.summary: Bryant said Liston and Randy Weston were so in tune that he never had to tell her anything.
items.notes: Liston: 'I don’t think so.'

items.pull_quote: Dig deep down and write. That’s a beautiful tune, Melba.
items.summary: Bryant called Liston's song Love, I've Found You a beautiful tune.
items.about: her song Love, I've Found You
items.notes: Liston: 'Thank you.'

items.pull_quote: Melba, looking around the walls here and seeing some of the many things – many awards and tributes that people have given you
items.summary: Bryant pointed to the many awards and tributes on Liston's walls before asking about her goals.
items.notes: Liston: 'No. I just went on and did whatever they told me to do.'

items.pull_quote: You just knew that you were going to be the best. You didn’t have to say it, right?
items.summary: Bryant suggested Liston had always known she would be the best without needing to say it.
items.notes: Liston: 'I didn’t know.' Bryant: 'Yes you did.' Liston: 'But I have to be the best that I can do.' (296350).

items.pull_quote: I’ll say for you: you have been the best, Melba. You’ve been a guiding light for a lot of people, including me
items.summary: Bryant told Liston she had been the best and a guiding light for many people, Bryant included.
items.about: what Liston meant to other musicians
items.notes: Liston goes straight to the advice question that follows in the same block.

items.pull_quote: But they still won’t have it as hard as you did.
items.summary: Bryant said young women musicians would not have it as hard as Liston had.
items.about: the hardships of her generation of women
items.notes: Liston: 'Oh no.'

items.pull_quote: But those schools that you helped organize and stuff like that, the kids wanted to learn, and they came there to learn, and they did learn, because you guys were teaching them.
items.summary: Bryant credited the schools Liston helped organise with children who wanted to learn and did.

items.pull_quote: Because Melba you’ve really overcome the stroke that you had. I think you’ve made a long stride, bettering yourself to overcome that
items.summary: Bryant told Liston she had really overcome her stroke and would do even greater things back East.
items.notes: Liston answers that she was afraid to go out and see anyone until six months earlier.

items.pull_quote: But see it’s your attitude that keeps it from being that way.
items.summary: Bryant said Liston's own attitude kept people from pitying her after the stroke.

items.pull_quote: you’ve taken it – your stroke in stride. I know a lot of people who’ve had it, and they’ve had that attitude, “Oh, woe is me.”
items.summary: Bryant said Liston had taken her stroke in stride, unlike others who fell into self-pity.
items.notes: Liston: 'I must have done that when I first . . .'

items.pull_quote: The quality is there though, Melba.
items.summary: Bryant told Liston that though she now wrote slowly the quality was still there.
items.notes: Liston continues her own sentence across it (296399).

items.pull_quote: But you did five things for me that I haven’t been able to see.
items.summary: Bryant mentioned five pieces Liston had written for her that she had not yet seen transcribed.

items.pull_quote: There’s no way the young girls today can understand the way we understand either.
items.summary: Bryant said young women musicians today could not understand what she and Liston understood.
items.about: the experience of their generation of women

items.pull_quote: They’re not going to go through what we went through to get – because there’s almost – we almost put it in their laps.
items.summary: Bryant said her and Liston's generation had almost put opportunity in the laps of today's young women.
items.about: their generation's legacy for women players

items.pull_quote: You have some dedicated friends back there, Melba. No jive. I know I’m dedicated, but you’ve got a whole big bunch of them out – back there.
items.summary: Bryant assured Liston that she had a big group of dedicated friends waiting in New York.
items.notes: Liston: 'That’s wonderful.'

items.pull_quote: because you’ve been such a major part of my life, really, and I’ve just – goose-bump time, your whole
items.summary: Bryant thanked the Smithsonian for letting her interview Liston, who had been a major part of her life.
items.notes: Sentence continues into 296504. Liston's reply comes after 296504: 'I’m sorry that I couldn’t talk more.'

items.pull_quote: how much I have admired you from afar – because you really didn’t know how much until of late. Maybe in the last year we became bonded, but I’ve been bonded to you a long time
items.summary: Bryant told Liston she had long admired her from afar and had felt bonded to her well before they became close.
items.notes: Same block: 'since you’ve had your stroke, this is just fantastic, Melba' and 'go back East and get ’em, girl. You go, girl.'

items.pull_quote: I know, but you’ve done – you’ve done it. You hear. You’ve done it to death.
items.summary: Bryant answered Liston's apology for not talking more by telling her she had done it to death.
